title: How Bogs Keep Bodies Safe for Thousands of Years
summary:
In August 1984, peat cutters near Wilmslow in England found a body in a peat bog. Known as the Lindow Man, he had lain there nearly 2,000 years, yet was still recognizable. He is one of at least 2,000 bog bodies found in Europe's peatlands.

A peat bog is a wet place made of peat, ground formed from partly decayed plants. Most peat is sphagnum moss, which stores water.

The wet moss leaves little air. Bogs get almost all their water from rain and snow, so they are low in minerals and the water barely moves. Without oxygen, the bog becomes acidic, and bacteria and fungi that break down dead material cannot thrive.

Instead, the acid pickles a body, like brine stopping harmful bacteria. Sphagnum moss also releases sphagnan, which protects skin and tissue, turning skin leathery and dark brown. Skin, hair, nails, and organs can stay intact for thousands of years.

Bones are different: acid takes calcium from them, so they can soften, bend, or dissolve. Raised bogs preserve bodies best, because they are highly acidic and oxygen-free.
why_it_matters: Learning how bogs preserve bodies helps you understand why some things from long ago survive while most things rot away.

keywords.explanation: Peat is soft, dark ground made from plants that have only partly rotted away in wet places.
Sphagnum is a kind of moss that soaks up and holds a lot of water.
Sphagnan is a substance released by sphagnum moss that helps protect skin and tissue.
Acidic means something is sour and sharp like vinegar, and it can slowly wear other materials away.
Calcium is a mineral that makes bones hard and strong.

background_read: A peat bog is a very wet place where dead plants pile up slowly and turn into a soft, dark material called peat.
Because bog water barely moves and has almost no air in it, the tiny living things that normally break down dead material cannot thrive there.
That is why a body in a bog can stay preserved instead of rotting away, with skin, hair, and organs lasting far longer than they would anywhere else.
Article_Structure: WHO: Peat cutters near Wilmslow in England, and the Lindow Man whose body they found.
WHAT: A body that had lain in a peat bog for nearly 2,000 years yet was still recognizable.
WHERE: In a peat bog near Wilmslow in England, one of Europe's peatlands.
WHY: Because bogs are wet, acidic, and almost free of oxygen, so bodies there are pickled and preserved instead of rotting away.
